title: The Gurdwara Act, 1925
hookLine: the law passes historic gurdwaras to an elected Sikh body

cards: A ballot paper, folded once, dropped into a box. It doesn't look like the end of a struggle. No march, no train on the rails, no police line.
Just a voter, a list of names, and a choice. But in the story of the gurdwara reform movement, that small, dull act is the prize.
For years Sikhs had walked into beatings and arrests to answer one question: who should care for the Guru's houses? The answer arrived in the plainest form there is.

teach.h: WHO CARES FOR THE GURU'S HOUSE?
teach.b: Through the campaigns at Nankana, Guru ka Bagh, Jaito and elsewhere, the reformers asked that historic gurdwaras be taken from hereditary mahants and returned to the sangat. The Sikh Gurdwaras Act was passed in Punjab.
It named historic gurdwaras and placed their management under a Sikh body whose members were chosen by Sikh voters. That body soon took the name the reformers had already made well-known: the SGPC.
Before, a shrine could pass from one mahant to his son or chosen disciple, like private property.

After, those who ran it answered to an elected committee, and the committee answered to the sangat at the ballot box. The movement didn't take the gurdwaras by force. It kept walking until the law changed.

teach.h: WHERE THE ONE NAME IS PRAISED.
teach.b: At Ang 72 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak asks how the true sangat can be known, and answers: it's where the One Name alone is praised.
The reformers' claim was that a gurdwara belongs to that sangat, not to a family, and the Act wrote that claim into law. It didn't settle every argument.
Sikhs have debated the elected body, its politics and its choices ever since, and still do.
But a debate held through votes and committees is itself part of what was won. A voter with a ballot paper is a strange kind of hero. At the end of this story, that's exactly who the hero is.

how: Historic gurdwaras in Punjab are managed under the Sikh Gurdwaras Act by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, whose members are elected by Sikh voters; its elections and decisions are discussed and debated across the community.

games.why: the struggle moved from police lines to ballot boxes: Sikh voters chose the body that would care for the historic gurdwaras.

practice: Bring to mind one place you hold in common with others, a gurdwara, a church, a library, a tenants' group, a town council: not yours alone, and not anyone else's alone either.
Picture the people who share it, and ask one quiet question: is there one way I could take part this month? If you pray, let Waheguru come on each breath out.
